title: October minutes reveal broad support for more tightening despite the hold
summary: October's 10–2 hold at 3.75–4.00% understated the support for a higher policy rate. The minutes of the 27–28 October meeting, released on 18 November, report that almost all participants considered further increases likely under their own baseline outlooks. Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack voted for an immediate quarter-point hike. A few hold supporters regarded the choice as close. Conversely, a few participants who preferred an increase could have accepted waiting if investors understood that further tightening remained likely. A couple thought even a move larger than 25 basis points at the next meeting might merit consideration if inflation data disappointed. That last view was conditional and narrow. The minutes do not say that a half-point move was the Committee's most likely next decision.

The published deliberations explain why a hold could still exert restraint. September's increase had already passed through promptly to overnight rates. Mortgage rates had risen and spreads for riskier borrowers had widened. Some participants thought the future rate increases embedded in market prices broadly matched their own assessment of an appropriate path. As long as those expectations persisted, longer financing terms could tighten before the next rate decision. Many wanted more information about the durability of AI investment, the state of credit, the effects of the September move and geopolitical developments. Advocates of acting sooner saw fewer benefits to delay: only limited data would arrive in the interval, overseas uncertainties could outlast it, and letting inflation become entrenched could require a larger adjustment later. The timing disagreement therefore turned partly on what credible communication could achieve in lieu of an immediate change.

The staff's economic review estimated annual September PCE inflation at 3.6%, with core inflation at 3.1%, from available consumer and producer price data. Several participants noted that annual revisions to the national accounts had reduced measured inflation during 2026. A couple cautioned that the change in measurement gave no reason on its own to improve the underlying outlook. High energy prices remained important, but participants reported pressure beyond directly affected products, including technology-related goods and market-based services excluding housing. Medium- and longer-term expectations appeared broadly consistent with 2%. Some also pointed out that market compensation based on CPI-indexed securities is difficult to interpret for a PCE objective when the two indices diverge unusually far. A stable market series is evidence about expectations, subject to a measurement caveat.

Staff expected energy inflation to moderate sharply the following year and tariff, geopolitical and AI-related contributions largely to fade over the next couple of years. Their forecast reached approximately 2% in 2028. They saw upside risks to that forecast, including the possibility that repeated above-target inflation had already changed expectations in ways available indicators might not fully capture. The near-term activity outlook was a little stronger than in September. Staff expected output to grow slightly faster than potential through 2028 and unemployment to stay below its longer-run staff estimate through 2029. Participants generally judged the labour market close to maximum employment, with risks more balanced. September unemployment was 4.2%, payroll gains averaged about 50,000 per month over three months and annual hourly earnings growth had slowed to 3%. Specialised workers on data-centre projects commanded wage premia while hiring and job-finding remained subdued elsewhere. Economy-wide wage acceleration was unnecessary for the inflation risks under discussion.

The Desk's market review supplies an especially clear example of the limits of an end-to-end yield change. Treasury yields climbed into early October on evidence of stronger activity. Later, doubts about revenues and financing needs at several AI companies, together with concern about French public finances, renewed demand for US Treasuries and reversed the rise. The ten-year French–German spread reached levels last seen around the 2011 euro-area crisis highs. US–foreign rate differentials widened and the dollar rose. Treasury liquidity deteriorated somewhat as volatility increased, but the manager judged trading remained orderly. Short-rate option volatility increased notably even as the expected US policy path changed little on net. A near-flat Treasury yield and a stable central estimate for rates could thus coexist with significant repricing of uncertainty.

Before the meeting, futures assigned little probability to an October increase but high probabilities to a quarter-point hike by year-end and two further moves by summer 2027. The median Desk survey participant expected increases in December and March, followed by a cut in early 2028. The survey's median estimate of the longer-run nominal funds rate rose to about 3.4%, which the manager associated with a higher estimate of the longer-run real rate. Term premia could account for part of the discrepancy between futures and surveys. These are investor and respondent assessments reported to the meeting. They are distinct from the policy path participants themselves considered appropriate and from investors' subsequent reaction to the detailed minutes.

The separate financial-stability briefing examined how a fall in expected returns on AI investment could travel from equity prices into funding. Some new capacity was financed through off-balance-sheet leases and circular arrangements between companies. Falling asset values could prompt leveraged investors to sell and funds facing redemptions to liquidate. Limited dealer capacity could then impair market functioning. Strong bank and household balance sheets provided some protection in the staff's scenarios. Participants nevertheless noted that supervisory data might miss indirect bank exposures through prime brokerage or credit lines to private credit funds. The potential for forced sales was a stress scenario. The Desk did observe a narrower development: high-yield bonds financing data-centre construction widened particularly sharply after revenue and financing news. That price change cannot establish that the broader forced-sale scenario had occurred.

The same distinction matters outside AI. The staff reported solid investment-grade issuance and a pickup in speculative-grade gross issuance, likely reflecting a need to refinance. Participants described more selective finance and reduced issuance for some lower-rated borrowers. Gross funds raised to meet maturities and access to new financing for a marginal project can move differently. Mortgage credit availability was easing gradually, yet high mortgage rates kept originations subdued. Credit standards, funding prices and volumes were therefore giving different but compatible signals. Reassessments of AI returns could damp investment demand and inflation even without a systemic disruption. They could also expose leveraged borrowers to losses, making the financial-stability outlook worse as some price pressures declined.

Money-market data gave the Desk little reason to change the reserve regime. Effective federal funds stayed two basis points below interest on reserves, and repo rates averaged slightly below that administered rate. The September corporate tax date and quarter-end passed without notable stress. The Desk kept reserve-management purchases at zero for the current purchase period, with monthly adjustments available if reserve conditions changed. The Board retained interest on reserves at 3.90% and primary credit at 4.00%. Participants also discussed readiness to use liquidity facilities and the distinction between purchases to restore market functioning and purchases intended to ease monetary conditions. These were preparatory discussions. The actual operating decision left both the rate range and the commitment to ample reserves in place.

An event study should locate the new information on 18 November. October's rate, named dissents and short statement had already been published. The broader support for additional restraint, the willingness of some hike supporters to wait under particular communication conditions, and the adverse AI-financing scenarios were part of what the fuller record disclosed. Its market figures concern the period ending before the October decision, not an observed return around release of the minutes.

questions.question: Did the minutes change the expected rate level, the timing of tightening or chiefly the upside tail?
questions.detail: Compare options and futures around 18 November, using maturities that distinguish the next meeting from summer 2027. Account for what had already become public since the October meeting. A higher probability of a larger move in adverse data need not imply a parallel rise across the curve or a higher most likely rate.

questions.question: Could an AI earnings disappointment transmit to the financial system through identifiable funding links?
questions.detail: Trace lease obligations, lender concentrations, credit facilities and collateral requirements for affected projects. Compare their spreads with similarly rated and duration-matched debt outside the sector. To establish amplification, look for redemptions, margin pressure, sales or lost market depth beyond the originally affected securities. Widening project spreads alone measure a change in pricing.

questions.question: Was expected restraint already affecting real demand where higher rates mattered most?
questions.detail: Compare mortgage offers with applications and originations, and distinguish refinancing issuance from funding for new business investment. Examine changes in rates, standards and quantities for otherwise similar borrowers. Weak housing alongside continued expansion by well-funded technology companies would help explain why confidence about transmission varied across participants.

questions.question: Did the inflation news change the economic outlook or its statistical representation?
questions.detail: Compare consistent vintages of PCE components, separating annual revisions from new monthly observations. Assess broad services prices, energy pass-through and technology bottlenecks, and allow for the CPI–PCE discrepancy in interpreting inflation compensation. A revised level by itself cannot settle whether the underlying tendency to raise prices has diminished.
